answers: "Any guy that can do a body-slam, he's my guy," President Trump shouted to a cheering Montana audience Thursday night as he simulated slamming someone to the ground, then noting, "I shouldn't say that." Trump was discussing Rep. Greg Gianforte, who assaulted Guardian reporter Ben Jacobs last year during the special election for the House seat vacated by Ryan Zinke, a misdemeanor assault to which he pleaded guilty and completed community service and an anger management class. Trump said after the incident, he feared Gianforte had blown his chance at the congressional seat. "I said, 'Oh, this is terrible, he's gonna lose the election,'" Trump recounted. "Then I said, 'Well, wait a minute—I know Montana pretty well. I think it might help him.' And it did." Trump was in Big Sky Country stumping for Matt Rosendale in his race for Democrat Jon Tester's Senate seat. Reaction came quickly: John Mulholland, US editor of the Guardian, put out a statement after the rally blasting Trump's words as "an attack on the First Amendment," asking for an apology and adding, "In the aftermath of the murder of Jamal Khashoggi, it runs the risk of inviting other assaults on journalists both here and across the world." ABC News reports on what the Toronto Star's Daniel Dale calls the "most significant" and "truly horrible" moment in the rally: "The president is gleefully applauding violence against a journalist." Trump also praised Gianforte as "smart" and then advised the crowd to "never wrestle him." (Trump seems to acknowledge Khashoggi is dead.)

Greg Gianforte, the newly elected congressman from Montana, has pleaded guilty to misdemeanor assault after an incident that occurred the night before the state's congressional election. The incident involved Gianforte body-slamming a reporter, Ben Jacobs, during a campaign event. Gianforte was sentenced to a 180-day deferred sentence, 40 hours of community service, 20 hours of anger management, a $300 fine, and a $85 court fee. The judge initially considered jail time but opted for community service and anger management due to eligibility restrictions for assault offenders. Gianforte has apologized to the journalist and pledged to donate $50,000 to the Committee to Protect Journalists.

President Donald Trump has expressed no regret for his comments praising Gianforte's actions, calling the incident a "tremendous success" and stating that Gianforte is a "great person" and "my type." Trump's comments have drawn criticism from the White House Correspondents' Association, which condemned the president for celebrating a violent act against a journalist. The association emphasized the importance of upholding the First Amendment and criticized Trump for undermining the role of the press.

Trump's visit to Montana was also focused on his campaign against Democratic Senator Jon Tester, who is running for re-election against Matt Rosendale. Trump has cited Tester's role in the failed nomination of White House physician Ronny Jackson as a reason for his opposition. Despite Trump's strong support, Tester maintains a slight lead in the polls, and the race has become one of the most expensive in Montana's history.

The news also includes several tweets about adding location information to tweets, which are not relevant to the main news stories. Overall, the news highlights the intersection of political campaigns, media freedom, and public reaction to controversial actions by public figures.
